opus-5.5.text:
My intuition is that they'll share a lot, but they won't be identical, and the differences matter.

The shared part is the backbone. The transformer has proven remarkably general. Whether you feed it text tokens, image patches, or video latents, it learns useful structure if you give it enough data and compute. So I don't think Physical AI needs to reinvent the core architecture from scratch. Reusing what works lets us benefit from all the engineering the community has already done on scaling, training stability, and inference efficiency.

The difference is in what the model has to represent and how it interacts with the world. A language agent mostly lives in a symbolic space: it reads text, reasons, calls a tool, gets text back. The physical world is continuous, high-dimensional, and governed by physics. A robot or an autonomous vehicle has to understand 3D space, object permanence, contact, dynamics, and cause and effect over time. It also has to act at a much higher frequency than a chatbot. You can't spend thirty seconds thinking before you catch a falling cup.

So I think about Physical AI as having a few pieces. First, a world model that understands and predicts how the physical world evolves. That's a big part of why we built Cosmos: video-based world foundation models that learn physical intuition from large amounts of real-world video. Second, a reasoning layer, which can look a lot like today's vision-language models and can borrow heavily from the LLM agent playbook: chain-of-thought, planning, common sense. Third, a policy or action layer that turns that understanding into motor commands, often with different tokenization, different time scales, and tight latency constraints.

In a sense, the architecture is probably a hierarchy: slow, deliberate reasoning on top, similar to current agents, and fast, reactive control at the bottom, which looks quite different. Humans work this way too. You plan your route consciously, but you don't consciously compute how to balance while walking.

The other big difference is data. Language agents were bootstrapped from the internet. Physical AI doesn't have an internet of robot action data. That's why I believe simulation and world models are so important: they let us generate the experience the model needs and test policies safely before they touch the real world. So even if the neural network blocks look similar, the training recipe and the data pipeline for Physical AI will look quite different.

To summarize: same family of building blocks, but a different system design, shaped by physics, real-time action, and the data problem.

r001.rationale: The response says Physical AI and existing agents share building blocks but need different system designs; it does not draw the specified analogy to using different tools for plowing versus weaving.

fable-5.1.text:
My intuition is: mostly yes at the foundation level, but not entirely, and the differences matter a lot.

Let me explain what I mean. If you look at the large language models and the agent systems built on top of them, the core recipe is pretty simple. You take a transformer, you pretrain it on a huge amount of data with a next-token objective, then you post-train it with supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning so it follows instructions and reasons. That recipe is extremely general. There is no reason it only applies to text. Video is just tokens, sensor readings are just tokens, actions are just tokens. So at the architecture level, I don't think physical AI needs something fundamentally new. The transformer, the scaling laws, the pretrain-then-post-train pipeline, those carry over.

But there are three places where physical AI is different, and I think these differences push you toward a different design even if the backbone looks the same.

The first is the data. Language models learned from the internet, which is basically humanity writing down its knowledge for thirty years. For the physical world, that doesn't exist. Nobody wrote down the physics of how a cup slides on a wet table or how a cable bends when you pull it. The knowledge is in video, in simulation, in robot trajectories, and most of it has to be generated or collected. So a physical AI model is really a world model first. It has to learn how the world evolves, how objects behave, how physics works, before it can learn to act. That's why we spent so much effort on video generation and world foundation models. You need a model that can imagine the next few seconds of the world, because that imagination is the equivalent of the knowledge an LLM gets from text.

The second is time and the control loop. An LLM agent can think for ten seconds, call a tool, think again. A robot operating in the real world cannot. It has to react at a very high frequency, sometimes hundreds of times per second, with latency constraints that a big reasoning model simply cannot meet. So in practice you end up with a hierarchy. A large model that reasons slowly about what to do, and a smaller, faster policy that actually produces motor commands. That is a structural difference. In the agent world the planner and the executor are often the same model called repeatedly. In physical AI I think they will be different models for a long time, connected through some intermediate representation, maybe language, maybe latent tokens, maybe predicted video.

The third is that the world is the training signal. For a language agent, the reward often comes from a human judge or a verifier. For physical AI, the environment itself tells you whether you succeeded. The cup fell or it didn't. That makes reinforcement learning more natural, but it also means you need a lot of simulation, because you cannot afford to break a thousand robots to learn one skill. And the quality of the simulation, the sim-to-real gap, becomes the bottleneck rather than the architecture.

So if I summarize my intuition: same backbone, same training philosophy, but a different data foundation centered on world models, a different system structure because of real-time constraints, and a much heavier dependence on simulation. I would say physical AI will borrow almost everything from the LLM playbook, and then add the pieces that come from the fact that the world has physics and clocks, and text does not.

r001.rationale: The response discusses shared foundations and design differences for Physical AI, but it does not compare the architectures to using different tools for plowing versus weaving.

astra-6.text:
My intuition is that they will share many of the same building blocks, but they don’t necessarily need exactly the same architecture. At a high level, both need to understand the situation, reason about what to do, and take actions. So there is a lot we can reuse.

But the physical world introduces different requirements. If a software agent takes a little longer to respond, that may be okay. For a robot interacting with a moving object, timing is part of whether the action succeeds. You also have to deal with continuous motion, uncertainty in sensing, and the consequences of your actions.

So I would expect some hierarchy: a model that reasons about the task and decides what should happen, coupled with a system that can execute and adjust quickly. Those could eventually be trained together. The key question for me is whether the architecture can learn the connection between perception, action, and how the world changes. I wouldn’t assume that an architecture that works well for a language agent automatically solves that.

r001.rationale: The response says Physical AI may need architecture adapted for timing, motion, and sensing, but it does not draw the plowing-versus-weaving tools analogy.

sol-6.1.text:
My intuition is that they will share some architectural ideas, but they won’t necessarily have exactly the same architecture. At a high level, both need to perceive, reason, plan, and take actions. So there’s a lot we can learn from existing agent models.

But physical AI has an additional challenge: you’re interacting with a world that changes continuously, and your actions have physical consequences. You need to understand motion, geometry, and how objects respond to forces. You also need feedback—you can’t just generate a plan and assume everything will happen as expected.

So I would expect some convergence at the reasoning and planning level, with specialized components for perception and control. The interesting question is how much of that can eventually be learned together in one model. I would keep that question open rather than assume today’s agent architecture is already the right answer.

r001.rationale: The response says Physical AI may need specialized perception and control components, but it does not draw the requested analogy to using different tools for plowing and weaving.
